blocking.finding: The attribution of clock04's fatal gap rests on a unit error. analyze_gc.py turns a pose stamp into a physics step with round(stamp_ns/1e6). The stamps are MuJoCo-Warp float32 time (physics_time() = mjw_data.time), which drifts away from steps x 1 ms: -43 ms at step 100,000, +451 ms at step 200,000 and +1,779 ms at step 387,640. Stamp 389.419128418 s is exactly physics step 387,640, not 389,419. The reported 79.7 ms 'Mac publish interval' therefore compares substeps that finished about 4.1 s after the backend had already received pose A. With the correct mapping, poses A (step 387,640) and B (step 387,675) were enqueued 278.6 ms apart. The control step that began 2.9 ms after A took 176.8 ms, with 58.3 ms of main-thread CPU, 465.5 ms of process runnable wait and an E-core share of 0.23; the external probe was up to 39 ms late. It was followed by a 119.7 ms step with 131.7 ms of wait. That is a mechanism-B slowdown. Six intermediate poses (not seven) were enqueued 83.5-244.5 ms after A and never reached the backend. By the script's own rule (Mac interval > 0.5 x gap means 'mac'), this gap is on the Mac side. So 'The Mac published on time: those two poses left the Mac 80 ms apart' is false, 'diag_v31_clock04 | C' is unsupported, and PLAN.md repeats both.

blocking.finding: Mechanism C is presented as a separate source, 'not in the worker at all', caused by the bridge's 10 ms publish callback running late. That location is inferred, not measured, and the corrected data point elsewhere. (i) Every frame the Mac sent reached the bridge and was accepted. In clock04, frames_sent was 79,538: 75,751 complete states accepted plus 3,787 clouds, with 0 telemetry reconnects and 0 io_errors. So the missing poses were superseded inside the bridge. Whether they arrived there late in a burst or the timer ran late is unmeasured. Late arrival could come from the worker's own lite3-telemetry-sender thread under the same host load, from Docker Desktop's host-VM networking, or from the bridge's telemetry thread. (ii) The bridge's simulation_clock_stall_events counter is driven by receipts in the telemetry thread (feedback_health.py), and it fired once in clock04. If that event is this gap, it favours late arrival over a late timer. (iii) Mapped through the clock offset, every backend gap over 150 ms with superseded poses falls in a B-type Mac step: 6 of 6 in clock04 (gaps of 151-297 ms, runnable wait 150-465 ms) and 7 of 7 in clock03 (runnable wait 136-429 ms). Gaps with consecutive stamps instead fall on process-wide stalls: in clock04, the 161 ms and 189 ms gaps match the logged 142.7 ms and 176.0 ms full collections; in clock03 they match the between-step freezes and the 265 ms in-process step. Superseding never occurred without B, which points to a shared host-load cause rather than an independent bridge mechanism.

blocking.where: versions/v32/PLAN.md 'Why this is enough' ('young-generation collections still run'), 'The known cost' and 'LiDAR kernel rebuild'; RESULT.md 'What v32 can and cannot change'; scripts/newton_episode.py lines 149-152 and 255-257
blocking.finding: The freeze schedule turns the per-scan kernel garbage into a permanent leak, and PLAN.md describes the effect wrongly. In clock04, over 18,939 steps, middle collections reclaimed 3,103,456 objects (median 4,964 per collection) and young collections 578,251. That is about 970 cyclic objects per scan. They are the temporary Module, Kernel, Adjoint and AST graphs that @wp.kernel(module='unique') builds and discards on every intersect_ray call (warp/_src/context.py 1896-2012); probe_scan_codegen shows none of them when the kernel is built once. In CPython 3.12.13, gc.freeze() resets all generation counters (checked: (452,4,0) -> (0,0,0)). With a freeze every 50 steps, full collections therefore never run and middle collections run at most about once per window. Garbage still pending at each freeze, and graphs still alive at it, are never reclaimed. In a scratch probe with the pinned kernel (launch patched out, 200 constructions), normal GC left 0.0 MB behind. With a freeze every 10 constructions, 163,236 objects were frozen, middle collections reclaimed nothing, and 28.1 MB remained after gc.collect(), about 0.14 MB per scan. At 10 scans per simulated second that is roughly 0.25-0.8 GB over a 390-600 s run. During clock03 the host's free memory had already fallen to about 2.7 GB, with swap-ins. 'The run is bounded, so this is bounded' does not register any bound.
blocking.evidence: The collected counts in gc_events.npy; probe_scan_codegen.json; a check of gc.get_count() before and after gc.freeze(); the scratch leak probe (tracemalloc); the vm counters in diag_v31_clock03's host.jsonl.
blocking.required_fix: Before freezing v32, do one of two things. Either call gc.collect() immediately before each gc.freeze(), which then traverses only the objects created since the previous freeze (measure its cost offline, then re-materialize and rerun K1 and K2). Or measure the leak in a worker-sized replay and pre-register an RSS bound and a stop rule. Correct PLAN.md and RESULT.md: full collections stop entirely, middle collections are curtailed, and the kernel rebuild that stays becomes the source of the leak.

non_blocking.finding: os_part = min(process runnable - process CPU, main-thread off-CPU) compares a sum over about 10 threads with one thread's off-CPU time. It was 10 ms late or less (its own p99) during all four clock03 freezes, which supports in-process holds. During B steps it was mostly 7-16 ms late with some 20-44 ms, so it does not confirm B.
